questions.sectionLabel: Growth, Development and Family-Centred Care
questions.stem: A four-year-old child becomes frightened when told that a blood sample is needed. Which nursing approach is most developmentally appropriate?

options.text: Use a doll to demonstrate the procedure, explain it in simple language, offer a limited choice and keep the parent nearby for reassurance.
Provide a detailed anatomical explanation and ask the child to remain still.
Ask the parent to hold the child firmly without explanation.
Delay all explanation until immediately before the needle is inserted.

questions.rationale: Preschool children benefit from simple language, demonstration, therapeutic play, limited choices and familiar support. These approaches reduce fear and improve cooperation.

questions.sectionLabel: Growth, Development and Family-Centred Care
questions.stem: An adolescent asks to speak with the nurse without a parent present. What is the best response?

options.text: Refuse because parents must always be present.
Provide an opportunity for private discussion where appropriate, explain confidentiality and its limits, and maintain respectful communication with the family.
Ask the adolescent to write concerns on a form.
Tell the adolescent that privacy is not part of paediatric care.

questions.rationale: Adolescents require privacy, respect and opportunities to communicate independently, while nurses explain confidentiality and legal limits.

questions.sectionLabel: Growth, Development and Family-Centred Care
questions.stem: A parent says, 'My toddler is normally active, but today he is unusually quiet and does not want to play.' Why is this information important?

options.text: Behaviour is less important than temperature.
Toddlers commonly become quiet when admitted, so no assessment is needed.
Parents often know the child's baseline behaviour and may recognise early deterioration.
Only the child's verbal report should guide assessment.

questions.rationale: Family observations are valuable because parents and carers usually know the child's normal behaviour best.

questions.sectionLabel: Growth, Development and Family-Centred Care
questions.stem: A child has not reached several expected language and motor milestones, and the parent reports loss of a skill previously acquired. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Reassure the parent that all children develop at the same rate eventually.
Wait until school age before reviewing development.
Focus only on the child's current weight.
Document the concern and arrange further developmental assessment.

questions.rationale: Variation occurs, but persistent delay or developmental regression requires further assessment.

questions.sectionLabel: Growth, Development and Family-Centred Care
questions.stem: Which statement best reflects family-centred paediatric care?

options.text: The child and family are partners in care, and their knowledge, preferences and needs are incorporated appropriately.
Parents should remain observers while professionals make all decisions.
Family involvement should occur only at discharge.
The same family role should be assumed for every child.

questions.rationale: Family-centred care values family knowledge, participation and preferences while maintaining the child's needs and safety.

questions.sectionLabel: Growth, Development and Family-Centred Care
questions.stem: A school-age child asks what will happen during a procedure. Which explanation is most suitable?

options.text: Avoid information to prevent anxiety.
Use honest, concrete language and explain the sequence in terms the child can understand.
Use only technical terminology.
Speak only to the parent.

questions.rationale: School-age children benefit from clear, truthful explanations that match their cognitive level.

questions.sectionLabel: Growth, Development and Family-Centred Care
questions.stem: A toddler refuses oral medication and becomes distressed. Which first approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Threaten an injection if the child refuses.
Mix the medicine secretly without checking safety.
Use calm simple language, involve the caregiver, offer a limited choice where possible and avoid deception.
Ask several staff members to restrain the child immediately.

questions.rationale: Developmentally appropriate communication and caregiver involvement can reduce distress. Deception damages trust, and restraint should not be the first response.

questions.sectionLabel: Growth, Development and Family-Centred Care
questions.stem: An infant has a chronological age of 10 months but was born very prematurely. How should development be interpreted?

options.text: Chronological age is the only factor that matters.
Milestones are not useful for premature infants.
The parent should compare the child only with siblings.
Development should be considered alongside age, prematurity and the child's individual abilities.

questions.rationale: Developmental assessment should consider chronological age, corrected age when relevant, and individual variation.

questions.sectionLabel: Growth, Development and Family-Centred Care
questions.stem: Which intervention best uses play as a clinical communication tool?

options.text: Allowing a child to explore safe equipment and rehearse a procedure with a toy.
Providing entertainment unrelated to care only.
Using play as a reward after every procedure.
Avoiding play because it may distract from assessment.

questions.rationale: Therapeutic play helps children understand care, express feelings and reduce fear.

questions.sectionLabel: Growth, Development and Family-Centred Care
questions.stem: A parent wants to perform a familiar comfort routine during a procedure. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Exclude the parent to preserve professional control.
Support the routine if it is safe and helpful to the child.
Allow it only after the procedure.
Ask another family to advise.

questions.rationale: Parents and carers can provide comfort and continuity and should be involved when safe and desired.

questions.sectionLabel: Growth, Development and Family-Centred Care
questions.stem: A preschool child repeatedly asks whether an injection is punishment for being 'bad.' What is the best nursing response?

options.text: Confirm that the injection is necessary because the child did not cooperate.
Ignore the question.
Explain simply that the medicine is to help the body and is not punishment.
Ask the parent to correct the child later.

questions.rationale: Young children may misunderstand illness and procedures. Clear reassurance prevents guilt and fear.

questions.sectionLabel: Growth, Development and Family-Centred Care
questions.stem: Which finding most strongly suggests developmental regression?

options.text: A child learns a new word more slowly than a sibling.
A child prefers one toy.
A child is shy with unfamiliar adults.
A child loses previously established speech or motor skills.

questions.rationale: Loss of previously acquired skills is a red flag requiring assessment.

questions.sectionLabel: Growth, Development and Family-Centred Care
questions.stem: A family declines a care activity because of a cultural practice that does not create clinical risk. What is the best response?

options.text: Ask about the practice and accommodate it where safe.
Insist on the usual routine.
Document non-compliance.
Avoid further discussion.

questions.rationale: Family-centred care requires respectful enquiry and safe accommodation rather than assumptions or judgement.

questions.sectionLabel: Growth, Development and Family-Centred Care
questions.stem: A nurse needs to assess an anxious toddler. Which sequence is most appropriate?

options.text: Begin with the most invasive examination.
Observe first, use play and caregiver support, and leave distressing parts until later when clinically safe.
Separate the child from the parent immediately.
Complete the assessment without speaking.

questions.rationale: Observation and a gradual, developmentally appropriate approach reduce distress and improve assessment quality.

questions.sectionLabel: Growth, Development and Family-Centred Care
questions.stem: A child with a developmental disability communicates using gestures rather than speech. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Assume the child cannot participate.
Direct all questions to the parent only.
Ask the family about the child's usual communication, use appropriate aids and observe behavioural cues.
Use standard verbal questions repeatedly.

questions.rationale: Communication should be adapted to individual ability, not based solely on chronological age.

questions.sectionLabel: Growth, Development and Family-Centred Care
questions.stem: Which outcome best demonstrates effective family-centred care?

options.text: The family follows instructions without asking questions.
The nurse makes all decisions quickly.
The parent remains outside the room.
The child and family understand the plan, contribute relevant information and participate in care according to preference and ability.

questions.rationale: Partnership, understanding and appropriate participation are key outcomes.

questions.sectionLabel: Growth, Development and Family-Centred Care
questions.stem: A child is fearful of staff after several painful procedures. Which action is most helpful?

options.text: Use consistent caregivers where possible, prepare the child honestly and use comfort and distraction strategies.
Approach quickly to complete tasks before resistance begins.
Promise that no procedure will hurt.
Avoid discussing previous experiences.

questions.rationale: Trust is supported by honest preparation, predictable care and developmentally appropriate coping strategies.

questions.sectionLabel: Growth, Development and Family-Centred Care
questions.stem: A parent reports concern about delayed speech, but another family member says, 'He will catch up.' What should the nurse do?

options.text: Dismiss the concern because family opinions differ.
Take the parent's concern seriously and assess development or refer according to local pathways.
Wait until adolescence.
Assess physical growth only.

questions.rationale: Parent concerns can be important indicators of developmental difficulty and should be evaluated.

questions.sectionLabel: Growth, Development and Family-Centred Care
questions.stem: What is the best way to involve an adolescent in care planning?

options.text: Speak only with the parent.
Require the adolescent to make all decisions alone.
Provide age-appropriate information, invite the adolescent's views and support growing autonomy within legal and developmental limits.
Avoid discussing sensitive topics.

questions.rationale: Adolescents should be included respectfully in decisions as their maturity and legal context allow.

questions.sectionLabel: Growth, Development and Family-Centred Care
questions.stem: Which outcome best reflects safe developmental nursing practice?

options.text: Every child receives the same explanation.
Only chronological age is considered.
Parents are involved only when the child cannot speak.
Assessment, communication and care are adapted to developmental stage, individual ability and family context.

questions.rationale: Safe paediatric care requires developmentally appropriate, individualised and family-centred practice.

questions.sectionLabel: Paediatric Assessment and Recognition of Deterioration
questions.stem: An infant with bronchiolitis is quieter than earlier, feeds poorly, has nasal flaring, chest retractions and fewer wet nappies. What is the nurse's priority?

options.text: Recognise respiratory and hydration deterioration, complete an urgent assessment and escalate promptly.
Reassure the parent that bronchiolitis commonly causes tiredness.
Offer a full bottle before reassessment.
Wait for the next scheduled observations.

questions.rationale: Behavioural change, respiratory distress and reduced urine output are significant signs of deterioration in an infant.

questions.sectionLabel: Paediatric Assessment and Recognition of Deterioration
questions.stem: Before touching a child, what should the nurse assess first?

options.text: Blood pressure only.
Appearance, interaction, breathing, colour, posture and response to the caregiver.
Pain score only.
The medical diagnosis.

questions.rationale: Observation before handling can reveal important signs of illness and distress.

questions.sectionLabel: Paediatric Assessment and Recognition of Deterioration
questions.stem: A quiet, floppy infant who responds poorly to a caregiver should be interpreted as:

options.text: A child who is simply tired.
A normal response to hospital admission.
A potentially seriously unwell child requiring prompt assessment.
Evidence of adequate pain control.

questions.rationale: Poor responsiveness and hypotonia are concerning paediatric signs.

questions.sectionLabel: Paediatric Assessment and Recognition of Deterioration
questions.stem: Why must paediatric vital signs be interpreted by age?

options.text: Children have identical normal ranges to adults.
Only temperature varies by age.
Age matters only for infants.
Normal heart rate, respiratory rate and blood pressure change with age.

questions.rationale: Age-specific ranges are essential because normal physiology changes throughout childhood.

questions.sectionLabel: Paediatric Assessment and Recognition of Deterioration
questions.stem: A non-verbal toddler is recovering from surgery. Which pain tool is most appropriate?

options.text: FLACC or another validated behavioural pain tool.
A numerical 0-10 scale only.
No pain tool is required.
An adult sedation score.

questions.rationale: FLACC supports pain assessment when verbal reporting is limited.

questions.sectionLabel: Paediatric Assessment and Recognition of Deterioration
questions.stem: A child has stridor at rest, suprasternal recession and increasing agitation. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Inspect the throat repeatedly.
Treat this as an airway emergency, minimise distress and seek urgent assistance.
Encourage the child to lie flat.
Offer oral food and fluids.

questions.rationale: Stridor at rest and increased work of breathing indicate significant upper-airway compromise.

questions.sectionLabel: Paediatric Assessment and Recognition of Deterioration
questions.stem: Which finding most strongly suggests dehydration in an infant?

options.text: Normal activity and moist mouth.
Increased urine output.
Reduced tears, dry mucous membranes, delayed capillary refill and fewer wet nappies.
Warm hands with brisk refill.

questions.rationale: Multiple hydration cues should be assessed together.

questions.sectionLabel: Paediatric Assessment and Recognition of Deterioration
questions.stem: A child is tachycardic but crying vigorously during observations. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Assume the result is normal and document it.
Use the adult normal range.
Ignore the heart rate.
Interpret the rate in context, settle the child if possible and repeat the assessment.

questions.rationale: Pain, fear and fever can affect vital signs, so readings should be interpreted in context and reassessed.

questions.sectionLabel: Paediatric Assessment and Recognition of Deterioration
questions.stem: Which change may be an early sign of paediatric deterioration?

options.text: Reduced feeding and altered behaviour.
Stable play and normal urine output.
Improved interaction.
A single request for sleep.

questions.rationale: Children may not describe symptoms clearly; behavioural and feeding changes can be early warning signs.

questions.sectionLabel: Paediatric Assessment and Recognition of Deterioration
questions.stem: A child with respiratory illness develops grunting and central cyanosis. What is the priority?

options.text: Routine reassessment in one hour.
Immediate airway and breathing assessment with urgent escalation.
Oral hydration first.
Discharge education.

questions.rationale: Grunting and central cyanosis are serious signs of respiratory compromise.

questions.sectionLabel: Paediatric Assessment and Recognition of Deterioration
questions.stem: A parent says, 'He is not himself, even though the monitor looks normal.' What should the nurse do?

options.text: Dismiss the concern because observations are normal.
Tell the parent to wait for the doctor.
Reassess the child and consider the parent's knowledge of baseline behaviour.
Document the comment only.

questions.rationale: Parents often identify subtle deterioration before objective values become severely abnormal.

questions.sectionLabel: Paediatric Assessment and Recognition of Deterioration
questions.stem: Which finding suggests poor circulation in a child?

options.text: Warm extremities and brisk refill.
Normal urine output.
Active play.
Prolonged capillary refill, cool extremities and altered responsiveness.

questions.rationale: These signs suggest impaired perfusion and require urgent assessment.

questions.sectionLabel: Paediatric Assessment and Recognition of Deterioration
questions.stem: A child with fever develops a non-blanching rash. What is the best nursing action?

options.text: Treat as a possible serious infection and escalate urgently.
Observe for several hours.
Apply moisturiser.
Ask the parent to photograph the rash.

questions.rationale: Fever with a non-blanching rash is a red flag requiring immediate action.

questions.sectionLabel: Paediatric Assessment and Recognition of Deterioration
questions.stem: A child has reduced consciousness after a seizure. What should the nurse assess first?

options.text: Meal intake.
Airway, breathing, circulation and neurological recovery.
School attendance.
Family history only.

questions.rationale: Immediate safety and physiological assessment take priority after a seizure.

questions.sectionLabel: Paediatric Assessment and Recognition of Deterioration
questions.stem: Which approach best assesses hydration comprehensively?

options.text: Assess thirst only.
Use urine colour only.
Review tears, mucous membranes, fontanel where relevant, capillary refill, urine output, weight and activity.
Check blood pressure only.

questions.rationale: No single sign is sufficient; hydration should be assessed using multiple cues.

questions.sectionLabel: Paediatric Assessment and Recognition of Deterioration
questions.stem: A child's respiratory rate increases over several hours while oxygen saturation remains within target. What should the nurse conclude?

options.text: The child is stable because saturation is normal.
The monitor is inaccurate.
No action is needed until cyanosis occurs.
Rising respiratory effort may be an early sign of deterioration and requires reassessment.

questions.rationale: Children can compensate before sudden decline; trend recognition is essential.

questions.sectionLabel: Paediatric Assessment and Recognition of Deterioration
questions.stem: A child is irritable, lethargic and has a bulging fontanel. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Recognise possible serious neurological illness and escalate urgently.
Reassure the parent.
Offer food.
Wait until the child sleeps.

questions.rationale: Bulging fontanel with neurological change is a red flag.

questions.sectionLabel: Paediatric Assessment and Recognition of Deterioration
questions.stem: Which outcome best indicates that an intervention for respiratory distress is effective?

options.text: A lower respiratory rate alone.
Reduced work of breathing, improved colour, alertness and oxygenation.
The child falls asleep.
The parent reports less anxiety.

questions.rationale: Response should be assessed using multiple clinical indicators.

questions.sectionLabel: Paediatric Assessment and Recognition of Deterioration
questions.stem: A child refuses to rate pain verbally. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Assume there is no pain.
Ask repeatedly until the child answers.
Use observation, caregiver input and an age-appropriate validated tool.
Document refusal only.

questions.rationale: Pain assessment should be adapted to developmental and communication ability.

questions.sectionLabel: Paediatric Assessment and Recognition of Deterioration
questions.stem: Which outcome best reflects effective paediatric assessment?

options.text: Only vital signs are recorded.
The nurse waits for the child to describe symptoms.
The same assessment sequence is used rigidly for every child.
The nurse identifies age-specific abnormalities, recognises behavioural change and escalates before sudden collapse.

questions.rationale: Effective paediatric assessment combines observation, age-specific interpretation and early action.

questions.sectionLabel: Nursing Care for Common Childhood Conditions
questions.stem: A school-age child with type 1 diabetes presents with vomiting, abdominal pain, deep breathing and increasing drowsiness. What is the priority?

options.text: Check glucose and ketones, assess hydration and activate urgent management for possible diabetic ketoacidosis.
Treat as gastroenteritis only.
Give food and wait.
Encourage exercise.

questions.rationale: Vomiting, abdominal pain, Kussmaul-type breathing and drowsiness are classic warning signs of DKA.

questions.sectionLabel: Nursing Care for Common Childhood Conditions
questions.stem: A child with croup has stridor only when upset and is otherwise alert. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Examine the throat with a tongue depressor.
Keep the child calm, assess airway and breathing, and monitor for progression.
Encourage crying to assess severity.
Place the child flat.

questions.rationale: Minimising distress is important because agitation can worsen upper-airway obstruction.

questions.sectionLabel: Nursing Care for Common Childhood Conditions
questions.stem: An infant with bronchiolitis is tiring during feeds and has increasing respiratory effort. What should the nurse prioritise?

options.text: Completing a full feed.
Routine discharge teaching.
Airway and breathing assessment, feeding safety and hydration review.
Encouraging prolonged crying.

questions.rationale: Respiratory fatigue and feeding difficulty increase risk of deterioration and aspiration.

questions.sectionLabel: Nursing Care for Common Childhood Conditions
questions.stem: A child with asthma becomes quieter with poor air entry despite less wheeze. What should the nurse suspect?

options.text: Improvement.
Resolution of bronchospasm.
Anxiety only.
Severe airflow limitation and fatigue.

questions.rationale: A quieter chest with reduced air entry can indicate worsening obstruction rather than improvement.

questions.sectionLabel: Nursing Care for Common Childhood Conditions
questions.stem: Which symptom in a child with gastrointestinal illness requires urgent surgical review?

options.text: Bilious vomiting.
Mild nausea.
One loose stool.
Temporary appetite loss.

questions.rationale: Bilious vomiting is a paediatric red flag and may indicate intestinal obstruction.

questions.sectionLabel: Nursing Care for Common Childhood Conditions
questions.stem: A child has intermittent severe abdominal pain and currant-jelly stool. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Treat as simple diarrhoea.
Recognise a possible urgent surgical condition and escalate immediately.
Encourage a large meal.
Wait for symptoms to resolve.

questions.rationale: Currant-jelly stool with episodic pain is a red flag for intussusception.

questions.sectionLabel: Nursing Care for Common Childhood Conditions
questions.stem: A child with congenital heart disease sweats and becomes breathless during feeds. What is the best nursing interpretation?

options.text: The child dislikes the formula.
This is normal teething behaviour.
Feeding may be creating significant cardiac workload and should be paced with clinical review.
The child should be encouraged to finish quickly.

questions.rationale: Poor feeding, sweating and breathlessness can indicate cardiac compromise.

questions.sectionLabel: Nursing Care for Common Childhood Conditions
questions.stem: Which nursing action best supports a child with heart failure?

options.text: Encourage vigorous activity.
Restrict all family contact.
Ignore feeding fatigue.
Pace activity and feeds, monitor breathing, growth and perfusion, and allow rest.

questions.rationale: Energy conservation and careful monitoring support children with reduced cardiac reserve.

questions.sectionLabel: Nursing Care for Common Childhood Conditions
questions.stem: A child with pneumonia becomes increasingly lethargic and requires more oxygen. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Recognise deterioration and escalate urgently.
Wait for the next antibiotic dose.
Reduce observations to allow rest.
Offer oral fluids only.

questions.rationale: Increasing oxygen requirement and lethargy suggest worsening respiratory illness.

questions.sectionLabel: Nursing Care for Common Childhood Conditions
questions.stem: A child with meningitis is suspected. Which finding is most concerning?

options.text: Mild headache with normal behaviour.
Fever with altered consciousness and a non-blanching rash.
Sore throat only.
Normal appetite.

questions.rationale: This combination may indicate severe invasive infection and requires immediate action.

questions.sectionLabel: Nursing Care for Common Childhood Conditions
questions.stem: During a seizure, which action is appropriate?

options.text: Restrain the child firmly.
Place an object in the mouth.
Protect the child from injury, maintain airway safety, time the seizure and observe features.
Offer oral medication during the seizure.

questions.rationale: Seizure care focuses on safety, airway and accurate observation.

questions.sectionLabel: Nursing Care for Common Childhood Conditions
questions.stem: A child remains drowsy and has abnormal breathing after a seizure. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Assume this is a normal postictal state.
Give food.
Leave the child to sleep alone.
Perform urgent ABC assessment and escalate.

questions.rationale: Persistent altered consciousness and abnormal breathing require urgent review.

questions.sectionLabel: Nursing Care for Common Childhood Conditions
questions.stem: A child with gastroenteritis has dry mucous membranes, prolonged capillary refill and minimal urine output. What is the priority?

options.text: Assess severity of dehydration and initiate prescribed rehydration or escalation.
Provide fruit juice only.
Delay care until vomiting stops.
Encourage normal activity.

questions.rationale: These findings indicate significant dehydration and possible circulatory compromise.

questions.sectionLabel: Nursing Care for Common Childhood Conditions
questions.stem: Which sign may indicate respiratory fatigue?

options.text: Loud crying with good colour.
Decreasing air entry with reduced effort and altered consciousness.
Improved interaction.
Normal feeding.

questions.rationale: A child may appear quieter as respiratory muscles tire; this is a late and dangerous sign.

questions.sectionLabel: Nursing Care for Common Childhood Conditions
questions.stem: A child with cystic fibrosis has increased cough, reduced appetite and weight loss. What should the nurse consider?

options.text: Normal variation.
Improved lung function.
Possible respiratory exacerbation and nutritional decline requiring review.
A minor behavioural issue.

questions.rationale: Cystic fibrosis affects both respiratory health and nutrition; changes require assessment.

questions.sectionLabel: Nursing Care for Common Childhood Conditions
questions.stem: Which outcome best indicates effective asthma treatment?

options.text: Wheeze disappears but the child becomes drowsy.
Respiratory rate falls while cyanosis develops.
The child sleeps deeply.
Improved air entry, reduced work of breathing and better ability to speak or play.

questions.rationale: Clinical improvement should include ventilation, effort and function.

questions.sectionLabel: Nursing Care for Common Childhood Conditions
questions.stem: A child with vomiting has a distended abdomen and severe pain. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Treat as a possible acute abdominal emergency and escalate.
Give a large meal.
Encourage walking.
Reassure the family.

questions.rationale: Severe pain and distension are red flags for obstruction or another surgical condition.

questions.sectionLabel: Nursing Care for Common Childhood Conditions
questions.stem: A child with type 1 diabetes becomes pale, shaky and confused. What is the priority?

options.text: Give insulin.
Check blood glucose and treat possible hypoglycaemia according to protocol.
Encourage sleep.
Wait for the next meal.

questions.rationale: These symptoms are consistent with hypoglycaemia and require rapid treatment.

questions.sectionLabel: Nursing Care for Common Childhood Conditions
questions.stem: Why should nurses monitor both the child and family during acute illness?

options.text: Family needs are unrelated to treatment.
Only the child's vital signs matter.
The child's condition and family understanding, coping and ability to continue care all affect outcomes.
Parents should not participate during illness.

questions.rationale: Paediatric care includes clinical support for the child and communication and education for the family.

questions.sectionLabel: Nursing Care for Common Childhood Conditions
questions.stem: Which outcome best reflects safe care for common childhood conditions?

options.text: The diagnosis is documented.
Only prescribed medication is given.
The same pathway is used without reassessment.
Red flags are recognised early, treatment response is monitored and the child and family receive appropriate support.

questions.rationale: Safe care integrates recognition, intervention, evaluation and family support.

questions.sectionLabel: Medication Safety, Nutrition and Child Protection
questions.stem: A toddler is prescribed 10 mg/kg of a medicine. The recorded weight is 22, but the nurse discovers it was entered in pounds rather than kilograms. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Pause administration, reweigh the child in kilograms, recalculate the dose and complete required checks.
Administer the calculated dose because the chart is official.
Convert 22 pounds to 22 kilograms.
Ask the parent to estimate the correct dose.

questions.rationale: Paediatric doses require a current weight in kilograms. A pounds-to-kilograms error can cause a serious overdose.

questions.sectionLabel: Medication Safety, Nutrition and Child Protection
questions.stem: Which information must be checked before administering a weight-based paediatric medicine?

options.text: Age only.
Current weight in kilograms, prescribed dose, concentration, route and maximum safe dose.
Tablet colour.
Parent preference only.

questions.rationale: Safe paediatric dosing requires several deliberate checks, often including independent verification.

questions.sectionLabel: Medication Safety, Nutrition and Child Protection
questions.stem: A child weighs 18 kg and is prescribed 5 mg/kg. What dose is required?

options.text: 23 mg.
90 mg.

questions.rationale: 5 mg multiplied by 18 kg equals 90 mg.

questions.sectionLabel: Medication Safety, Nutrition and Child Protection
questions.stem: Why is independent verification often required for paediatric medicines?

options.text: Children always refuse medicines.
Parents cannot provide consent.
Paediatric medicines are never standardised.
Small calculation or concentration errors can cause serious harm.

questions.rationale: Children have small therapeutic margins, and weight-based calculations increase error risk.

questions.sectionLabel: Medication Safety, Nutrition and Child Protection
questions.stem: A child's current weight is unavailable, but a medication dose is due. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Obtain or verify a current weight before calculation unless an emergency protocol provides another safe method.
Use the weight from a sibling.
Estimate by age.
Administer half the adult dose.

questions.rationale: Accurate dosing requires a verified current weight.

questions.sectionLabel: Medication Safety, Nutrition and Child Protection
questions.stem: Which assessment best evaluates a child's nutrition and growth?

options.text: One weight measurement only.
Growth chart trend, dietary history, feeding observation and clinical assessment.
Parent opinion only.
Height only.

questions.rationale: Growth and nutrition should be evaluated over time using multiple sources.

questions.sectionLabel: Medication Safety, Nutrition and Child Protection
questions.stem: A child crosses downward through several growth percentiles. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Assume this is normal variation.
Increase calorie intake without assessment.
Assess feeding, health, psychosocial factors and arrange further review.
Wait until adolescence.

questions.rationale: A sustained change in growth trajectory may indicate nutritional, medical or social concerns.

questions.sectionLabel: Medication Safety, Nutrition and Child Protection
questions.stem: Which injury-prevention advice is most appropriate for a toddler?

options.text: Sport helmet education only.
Independent road crossing.
Sleeping with loose bedding.
Safe storage of medicines and poisons, supervision near water and age-appropriate car restraint.

questions.rationale: Injury prevention should match the child's developmental risks.

questions.sectionLabel: Medication Safety, Nutrition and Child Protection
questions.stem: Which safe-sleep advice is most appropriate for an infant?

options.text: Use a safe sleep surface and follow local recommendations regarding position and bedding.
Place the infant prone with pillows.
Use loose blankets and soft toys.
Allow sleeping on a sofa.

questions.rationale: Safe sleep education reduces preventable infant harm and should follow current local guidance.

questions.sectionLabel: Medication Safety, Nutrition and Child Protection
questions.stem: A child has bruises in unusual locations that do not match the caregiver's explanation. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Confront the caregiver aggressively.
Document objectively, ensure immediate safety and follow legal and organisational safeguarding procedures.
Ignore the concern without proof.
Ask the child to return alone later.

questions.rationale: Inconsistent injuries may indicate abuse. Nurses should document and report through approved pathways rather than investigate independently.

questions.sectionLabel: Medication Safety, Nutrition and Child Protection
questions.stem: Which finding may indicate neglect?

options.text: A single accidental scrape.
A parent asking questions.
Persistent poor hygiene, untreated health needs and inadequate supervision.
A child being shy.

questions.rationale: Neglect may be reflected in unmet basic health, hygiene, nutrition or safety needs.

questions.sectionLabel: Medication Safety, Nutrition and Child Protection
questions.stem: A caregiver delays seeking care for a serious injury and gives changing explanations. What is the best nursing response?

options.text: Assume stress caused the inconsistency.
Wait for another incident.
Discuss the case with other families.
Consider safeguarding concerns, document facts and follow reporting requirements.

questions.rationale: Delayed presentation and inconsistent explanations are safeguarding red flags.

questions.sectionLabel: Medication Safety, Nutrition and Child Protection
questions.stem: Which documentation is most appropriate for a suspected safeguarding concern?

options.text: Objective descriptions of injuries, statements and observed behaviour without speculation.
A diagnosis of abuse without assessment.
Emotional language.
No documentation until the case is proven.

questions.rationale: Accurate, factual documentation supports safe and lawful follow-up.

questions.sectionLabel: Medication Safety, Nutrition and Child Protection
questions.stem: A parent asks how to prevent poisoning at home. What advice is best?

options.text: Keep products under the sink.
Store medicines and chemicals locked, out of reach and in original containers.
Transfer chemicals into drink bottles.
Teach toddlers to avoid them.

questions.rationale: Environmental controls are more reliable than relying on a young child's understanding.

questions.sectionLabel: Medication Safety, Nutrition and Child Protection
questions.stem: A child with feeding difficulty coughs during meals and has poor weight gain. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Encourage faster feeding.
Ignore coughing if the child finishes meals.
Assess feeding safety and refer for appropriate multidisciplinary review.
Recommend unrestricted foods.

questions.rationale: Coughing with feeding and poor growth may indicate swallowing or nutritional difficulty.

questions.sectionLabel: Medication Safety, Nutrition and Child Protection
questions.stem: Which approach best supports an adolescent with obesity?

options.text: Focus only on appearance.
Recommend extreme dieting.
Exclude the adolescent from planning.
Use respectful, non-stigmatising assessment of nutrition, activity, health and family context.

questions.rationale: Nutrition care should be respectful, developmentally appropriate and evidence-informed.

questions.sectionLabel: Medication Safety, Nutrition and Child Protection
questions.stem: A medication calculation result seems unusually high for a small child. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Stop, recheck weight, units, dose and concentration, and obtain independent verification.
Administer it because the formula was used.
Round the dose upward.
Ask the parent if it looks correct.

questions.rationale: A reasonableness check is essential in paediatric medication safety.

questions.sectionLabel: Medication Safety, Nutrition and Child Protection
questions.stem: Which outcome best demonstrates effective injury-prevention education?

options.text: A leaflet is provided.
The family can explain and apply age-specific safety measures in the home and community.
The parent signs a form.
The child promises to be careful.

questions.rationale: Understanding and practical application are more meaningful than information delivery alone.

questions.sectionLabel: Medication Safety, Nutrition and Child Protection
questions.stem: What is the nurse's responsibility when abuse or neglect is suspected?

options.text: Investigate the family independently.
Wait for certainty.
Follow legal and organisational reporting requirements while supporting the child's immediate safety.
Discuss the case publicly.

questions.rationale: Nurses must act within safeguarding laws and policies and should not delay until proof is established.

questions.sectionLabel: Medication Safety, Nutrition and Child Protection
questions.stem: Which outcome best reflects safe practice in medication, nutrition and child protection?

options.text: Only medication calculations are correct.
Families receive general advice only.
Safeguarding concerns are managed informally.
Weight-based medicines are verified, growth concerns are assessed, injury prevention is tailored and safeguarding concerns are reported appropriately.

questions.rationale: Safe paediatric practice integrates medication safety, growth, prevention and protection.

questions.sectionLabel: Advanced Paediatric Assessment and Prioritisation
questions.stem: A 6-year-old is drowsy after minor surgery. The heart rate and blood pressure remain within the expected range for age, but the child is increasingly difficult to rouse and the respiratory rate has fallen from 22 to 10 breaths per minute. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Recognise possible opioid-related respiratory depression, assess airway and breathing, and escalate immediately.
Allow the child to sleep and repeat observations in 30 minutes.
Ask the parent whether the child usually sleeps deeply.
Document the findings and wait for the surgical team.

questions.rationale: A falling respiratory rate with reduced responsiveness is more important than otherwise normal observations and may indicate opioid toxicity. Airway, breathing and urgent escalation take priority.

questions.sectionLabel: Advanced Paediatric Assessment and Prioritisation
questions.stem: The parent of a toddler says, 'She is not herself today.' The toddler's temperature is 37.4°C and oxygen saturation is 97%, but she is unusually quiet and not making eye contact. What is the most appropriate nursing response?

options.text: Reassure the parent because the recorded observations are normal.
Complete a focused assessment and compare current behaviour with the child's normal baseline.
Ask the parent to observe the child at home.
Wait until a vital sign becomes abnormal.

questions.rationale: Caregiver concern and altered interaction may precede measurable deterioration. The child should be assessed rather than dismissed because individual observations are normal.

questions.sectionLabel: Advanced Paediatric Assessment and Prioritisation
questions.stem: Which assessment approach best applies the paediatric assessment triangle?

options.text: Measure blood pressure, temperature and weight only.
Complete a head-to-toe examination before observing behaviour.
Evaluate appearance, work of breathing and circulation to the skin before beginning a detailed examination.
Ask the caregiver to identify the diagnosis.

questions.rationale: The paediatric assessment triangle provides a rapid first impression based on appearance, breathing and circulation.

questions.sectionLabel: Advanced Paediatric Assessment and Prioritisation
questions.stem: A 3-year-old with gastroenteritis has a heart rate of 148 beats per minute, dry mucous membranes, capillary refill of 4 seconds and markedly reduced urine output. Blood pressure is still within the expected range. How should the nurse interpret these findings?

options.text: The child is stable because hypotension is absent.
The elevated heart rate is most likely due to anxiety alone.
Oral intake can be deferred until the next shift.
The child may have significant dehydration and compensated shock requiring urgent review.

questions.rationale: Children may maintain blood pressure until late in shock. Tachycardia, delayed refill and reduced urine output suggest compromised perfusion.

questions.sectionLabel: Advanced Paediatric Assessment and Prioritisation
questions.stem: An adolescent with chronic illness asks to discuss a new symptom without a parent present. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Provide a private opportunity, explain confidentiality and its limits, and assess the concern respectfully.
Refuse because parents must hear all clinical information.
Ask the adolescent to submit the concern in writing.
Inform the parent before hearing the adolescent's concern.

questions.rationale: Adolescents should be given appropriate privacy while the nurse explains legal and safety limits to confidentiality.

questions.sectionLabel: Advanced Paediatric Assessment and Prioritisation
questions.stem: A 4-month-old infant is admitted with respiratory illness. Which observation is most concerning?

options.text: The infant cries during examination.
The infant is quiet, has poor eye contact and responds weakly to the caregiver.
The respiratory rate rises briefly while feeding.
The infant sleeps between feeds.

questions.rationale: A quiet, poorly responsive infant may be seriously unwell. Appearance and interaction are central to paediatric assessment.

questions.sectionLabel: Advanced Paediatric Assessment and Prioritisation
questions.stem: The nurse is preparing an ISBAR escalation for a deteriorating child. Which information is essential to include?

options.text: The diagnosis and bed number only.
A complete account of every event since admission.
The child's name, age, current weight, clinical concern, relevant history, assessment findings and required action.
The parent's opinion without objective assessment.

questions.rationale: Paediatric escalation should clearly identify the child, age and weight, describe the concern and findings, and state the action required.

questions.sectionLabel: Advanced Paediatric Assessment and Prioritisation
questions.stem: A child's respiratory rate has risen gradually over four hours, although oxygen saturation remains within the target range. What is the best nursing action?

options.text: Conclude that the child is stable because saturation is acceptable.
Reduce the frequency of observations.
Wait for cyanosis before seeking review.
Assess work of breathing, compare trends and escalate if the pattern is concerning.

questions.rationale: Tachypnoea may be an early sign of deterioration. Normal saturation does not exclude increasing respiratory effort or fatigue.

questions.sectionLabel: Advanced Paediatric Assessment and Prioritisation
questions.stem: Which finding most strongly suggests impaired circulation in a child?

options.text: Cool mottled skin, capillary refill of 5 seconds and reduced responsiveness.
Warm extremities, brisk capillary refill and normal interaction.
A single episode of crying.
Mild tachycardia immediately after activity.

questions.rationale: Cool mottled skin, delayed refill and altered responsiveness indicate poor perfusion.

questions.sectionLabel: Advanced Paediatric Assessment and Prioritisation
questions.stem: A child refuses to use a numerical pain scale. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Record that pain cannot be assessed.
Use an age-appropriate validated tool, behavioural observation and caregiver input.
Assume there is no pain because the child will not score it.
Ask the parent to choose a number on the child's behalf.

questions.rationale: Pain assessment should be adapted to age, development and communication ability rather than abandoned.

questions.sectionLabel: Advanced Paediatric Assessment and Prioritisation
questions.stem: A parent repeatedly reports that a child is deteriorating, but the paediatric early-warning score remains below the escalation threshold. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Wait until the score reaches the trigger level.
Advise the parent that the score is objective.
Reassess the child and escalate based on clinical concern and caregiver information.
Document the concern without further action.

questions.rationale: Scoring tools support but do not replace clinical judgement. Caregiver concern is an important safety signal.

questions.sectionLabel: Advanced Paediatric Assessment and Prioritisation
questions.stem: A 7-year-old's pulse is elevated while crying during a painful procedure. Which nursing action is most appropriate?

options.text: Interpret the pulse as evidence of shock.
Use adult normal ranges.
Ignore the pulse because children often cry.
Settle the child, reassess pain and repeat observations when possible.

questions.rationale: Vital signs should be interpreted within age and context. Reassessment after distress is reduced improves accuracy.

questions.sectionLabel: Advanced Paediatric Assessment and Prioritisation
questions.stem: Which statement best explains why hypotension is a late sign in paediatric shock?

options.text: Children can maintain blood pressure through compensatory tachycardia and vasoconstriction until circulatory failure is advanced.
Children normally have very low blood pressure.
Blood pressure does not reflect circulation in children.
Hypotension occurs only in dehydration.

questions.rationale: Children may compensate effectively before sudden decompensation, so earlier signs must be recognised.

questions.sectionLabel: Advanced Paediatric Assessment and Prioritisation
questions.stem: A toddler becomes increasingly irritable, then lethargic, during an assessment. What is the safest interpretation?

options.text: The child is becoming accustomed to the ward.
The change may indicate neurological or systemic deterioration and requires reassessment.
The child is probably tired from crying.
The parent should settle the child before any further assessment.

questions.rationale: A progression from irritability to lethargy can be a serious sign and should prompt urgent assessment.

questions.sectionLabel: Advanced Paediatric Assessment and Prioritisation
questions.stem: What is the main advantage of observing a child before touching them?

options.text: It eliminates the need for physical examination.
It is useful only in infants.
It allows assessment of appearance, breathing, posture and interaction before distress alters findings.
It avoids involving the caregiver.

questions.rationale: Observation first provides valuable information in the child's least disturbed state.

questions.sectionLabel: Advanced Paediatric Assessment and Prioritisation
questions.stem: A 9-year-old with a neurological condition has a new unequal pupil response and worsening headache. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Provide simple analgesia and reassess later.
Ask the child to rest in a dark room.
Wait for vomiting to occur.
Perform urgent neurological assessment and escalate immediately.

questions.rationale: New pupillary change and worsening headache may indicate raised intracranial pressure or another acute neurological event.

questions.sectionLabel: Advanced Paediatric Assessment and Prioritisation
questions.stem: A paediatric early-warning tool generates a low score, but the child has poor feeding and reduced wet nappies. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Assess hydration and overall condition, and escalate if the findings are concerning.
Disregard the symptoms because the score is low.
Encourage the family to keep a diary.
Wait until the child becomes hypotensive.

questions.rationale: Early deterioration may appear through feeding and urine-output changes before the score rises.

questions.sectionLabel: Advanced Paediatric Assessment and Prioritisation
questions.stem: Which assessment finding should take priority over routine documentation?

options.text: A stable child awaiting discharge instructions.
A child with new grunting and marked chest retractions.
A parent asking about visiting hours.
A child due for a routine weight check.

questions.rationale: New respiratory distress is an immediate priority.

questions.sectionLabel: Advanced Paediatric Assessment and Prioritisation
questions.stem: A nurse escalates a concern but receives a response that does not match the child's worsening condition. What should happen next?

options.text: Wait for the original clinician to review the child.
Ask the parent to call another service.
Continue escalation through the approved pathway while providing ongoing care.
Document the delay and stop.

questions.rationale: Escalation should continue until the response matches the urgency of the child's condition.

questions.sectionLabel: Advanced Paediatric Assessment and Prioritisation
questions.stem: Which outcome best demonstrates effective advanced paediatric assessment?

options.text: All vital signs are recorded.
The nurse follows the score without variation.
The child remains calm during assessment.
The nurse integrates age, development, trends and caregiver concerns, then acts before severe deterioration occurs.

questions.rationale: Advanced assessment combines structured tools with clinical judgement and early action.

questions.sectionLabel: Managing High-Risk Paediatric Conditions
questions.stem: A child with severe asthma becomes quieter, can speak only one or two words at a time, and has markedly reduced air entry despite treatment. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Recognise impending respiratory failure, support airway and breathing, and escalate urgently.
Interpret the reduced wheeze as improvement.
Encourage the child to walk to improve ventilation.
Delay review until oxygen saturation falls further.

questions.rationale: A quiet chest, poor speech and reduced air entry indicate severe obstruction and fatigue, not recovery.

questions.sectionLabel: Managing High-Risk Paediatric Conditions
questions.stem: A 2-year-old with suspected upper-airway obstruction has stridor at rest and increasing suprasternal recession. Which nursing action is most appropriate?

options.text: Inspect the throat with a tongue depressor.
Keep the child calm, minimise distress and obtain urgent airway support.
Ask the child to lie flat.
Offer oral fluids.

questions.rationale: Distress can worsen upper-airway obstruction. Calm handling and urgent airway support are priorities.

questions.sectionLabel: Managing High-Risk Paediatric Conditions
questions.stem: A child with fever develops a non-blanching rash, prolonged capillary refill and lethargy. Blood pressure remains normal. What is the priority?

options.text: Wait for hypotension to confirm shock.
Apply a topical cream and observe.
Activate the sepsis pathway and support urgent assessment and treatment.
Encourage oral fluids only.

questions.rationale: Normal blood pressure does not exclude paediatric shock. The pattern is concerning for sepsis and poor perfusion.

questions.sectionLabel: Managing High-Risk Paediatric Conditions
questions.stem: During a prolonged seizure, which nursing action has the highest priority?

options.text: Offer oral rescue medication immediately.
Restrain the child's limbs.
Ask the parent to hold the child still.
Protect the airway, maintain safety, time the seizure and activate the emergency response.

questions.rationale: Airway protection, safety and timely emergency management are the priorities during a prolonged seizure.

questions.sectionLabel: Managing High-Risk Paediatric Conditions
questions.stem: A child with meningitis is becoming less responsive and has repeated vomiting. What complication should the nurse consider?

options.text: Raised intracranial pressure.
Simple dehydration only.
Improving neurological status.
Medication refusal.

questions.rationale: Reduced consciousness and vomiting may indicate increasing intracranial pressure.

questions.sectionLabel: Managing High-Risk Paediatric Conditions
questions.stem: A child with severe dehydration remains tachycardic and poorly perfused after initial fluid treatment. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Assume the child needs more oral fluids only.
Reassess response and escalate urgently because shock may be persisting.
Wait until blood pressure falls.
Stop monitoring to reduce distress.

questions.rationale: Failure to improve after treatment is clinically significant and requires urgent reassessment.

questions.sectionLabel: Managing High-Risk Paediatric Conditions
questions.stem: Which finding is most consistent with worsening paediatric shock?

options.text: Improved interaction and warm skin.
Normal capillary refill.
Increasing lethargy, cool extremities and declining urine output.
Stable feeding.

questions.rationale: Neurological change, vasoconstriction and oliguria indicate worsening perfusion.

questions.sectionLabel: Managing High-Risk Paediatric Conditions
questions.stem: A child with diabetic ketoacidosis is receiving fluids and insulin. Which monitoring is most important?

options.text: Temperature only.
Dietary intake only.
Weight once daily.
Glucose, electrolytes, neurological status, hydration and treatment response.

questions.rationale: DKA treatment can cause rapid metabolic changes and cerebral complications, requiring close monitoring.

questions.sectionLabel: Managing High-Risk Paediatric Conditions
questions.stem: A child with DKA develops a sudden headache, bradycardia and reduced consciousness. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Recognise possible cerebral oedema and escalate immediately.
Continue treatment unchanged.
Give oral glucose.
Encourage sleep.

questions.rationale: Neurological deterioration during DKA treatment may indicate cerebral oedema, a medical emergency.

questions.sectionLabel: Managing High-Risk Paediatric Conditions
questions.stem: Which intervention is appropriate for a child with respiratory failure?

options.text: Rely only on pulse oximetry.
Provide oxygenation support, monitor ventilation and prepare for advanced escalation.
Encourage oral feeding during distress.
Delay specialist involvement.

questions.rationale: Respiratory failure requires immediate support and preparation for higher-level care.

questions.sectionLabel: Managing High-Risk Paediatric Conditions
questions.stem: A child with suspected sepsis has tachycardia, altered behaviour and reduced urine output. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Hypotension must be present before treatment begins.
The findings are expected with fever.
These are important early signs and urgent action is required.
Only the urine output is abnormal.

questions.rationale: Tachycardia, behaviour change and oliguria may precede hypotension in paediatric shock.

questions.sectionLabel: Managing High-Risk Paediatric Conditions
questions.stem: A child with a head injury becomes increasingly irritable and vomits twice. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Provide food and observe.
Allow uninterrupted sleep.
Ask the parent to continue home observation.
Perform urgent neurological reassessment and escalate.

questions.rationale: New neurological symptoms following head injury require urgent reassessment.

questions.sectionLabel: Managing High-Risk Paediatric Conditions
questions.stem: Which finding suggests respiratory fatigue rather than improvement?

options.text: A reduction in respiratory effort accompanied by drowsiness and poor air entry.
Less anxiety with improved air entry.
Normal speech and colour.
Reduced retractions with stable alertness.

questions.rationale: Apparent reduction in effort with worsening alertness and airflow can indicate exhaustion.

questions.sectionLabel: Managing High-Risk Paediatric Conditions
questions.stem: A child with severe electrolyte disturbance develops muscle weakness and an irregular cardiac rhythm. What is the priority?

options.text: Routine review tomorrow.
Urgent cardiac and clinical assessment with escalation.
Encourage activity.
Delay treatment until repeat symptoms occur.

questions.rationale: Severe electrolyte abnormalities can cause life-threatening arrhythmias.

questions.sectionLabel: Managing High-Risk Paediatric Conditions
questions.stem: A child with suspected meningococcal infection is deteriorating rapidly. Which communication is most appropriate?

options.text: A detailed account of the entire admission.
A message that the child 'looks unwell.'
A concise escalation that includes age, weight, current concern, perfusion findings and urgent action required.
A request for routine review.

questions.rationale: Clear, specific and urgent communication supports timely action.

questions.sectionLabel: Managing High-Risk Paediatric Conditions
questions.stem: A child treated for anaphylaxis remains wheezy and hypotensive. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Assume improvement will occur with time.
Offer oral fluids.
Stop monitoring after the first treatment.
Continue emergency management and escalate because the response is inadequate.

questions.rationale: Persistent airway and circulatory compromise requires ongoing emergency treatment.

questions.sectionLabel: Managing High-Risk Paediatric Conditions
questions.stem: Which action best evaluates the effectiveness of emergency treatment?

options.text: Reassess airway, breathing, circulation, neurological status and vital-sign trends.
Check only whether medication was given.
Ask the caregiver if the child looks better.
Document the intervention before reassessment.

questions.rationale: Treatment effectiveness must be determined through repeated clinical assessment.

questions.sectionLabel: Managing High-Risk Paediatric Conditions
questions.stem: A child with severe asthma has an oxygen saturation of 95% but is exhausted and barely moving air. What is the best interpretation?

options.text: The saturation proves the child is stable.
Clinical signs suggest severe respiratory compromise despite the saturation.
The child should be discharged.
No further treatment is required.

questions.rationale: Pulse oximetry may remain acceptable while ventilation and effort deteriorate.

questions.sectionLabel: Managing High-Risk Paediatric Conditions
questions.stem: Which patient requires the most urgent assessment?

options.text: A child with mild chronic eczema.
A child requesting pain medication for a stable injury.
A child with fever and a non-blanching rash.
A child awaiting routine discharge.

questions.rationale: Fever with a non-blanching rash may indicate life-threatening infection.

questions.sectionLabel: Managing High-Risk Paediatric Conditions
questions.stem: Which outcome best reflects safe management of a high-risk paediatric condition?

options.text: The diagnosis is recorded.
The family is informed after treatment.
The protocol is completed without deviation.
The nurse recognises the emergency pattern, initiates age-appropriate intervention and reassesses continuously.

questions.rationale: Safe management requires recognition, intervention, escalation and ongoing evaluation.

questions.sectionLabel: Complex Medication, Chronic Illness and Discharge Care
questions.stem: A child with epilepsy is being discharged with rescue medication. Which action best confirms that both caregivers can manage an emergency safely?

options.text: Check the dose against current weight, provide a written plan and require each caregiver to demonstrate administration.
Provide a leaflet and ask whether they understand.
Ask one caregiver to teach the other at home.
Rely on previous experience.

questions.rationale: Teach-back and return demonstration provide stronger evidence of understanding than verbal agreement alone.

questions.sectionLabel: Complex Medication, Chronic Illness and Discharge Care
questions.stem: A child's weight has increased significantly since the last admission. What should the nurse do before administering a weight-based medicine?

options.text: Use the previous dose because the medicine is unchanged.
Confirm the current weight in kilograms and recalculate the dose and maximum safe limit.
Ask the parent to estimate the new dose.
Round the previous dose upward.

questions.rationale: Paediatric doses should be recalculated when weight changes.

questions.sectionLabel: Complex Medication, Chronic Illness and Discharge Care
questions.stem: A smart infusion pump accepts a rate that appears unusually high for a small child. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Trust the pump because it has safety software.
Reduce the rate by half without clarification.
Stop and independently verify the order, concentration, weight, rate and maximum dose.
Ask the parent whether the rate is familiar.

questions.rationale: Technology supports but does not replace independent verification or reasonableness checks.

questions.sectionLabel: Complex Medication, Chronic Illness and Discharge Care
questions.stem: A medication order is written in micrograms, but the available concentration is labelled in milligrams. What is the safest action?

options.text: Convert mentally and administer immediately.
Round to the nearest milligram.
Ask another nurse to sign after administration.
Complete a careful unit conversion, verify the calculation independently and clarify any uncertainty before administration.

questions.rationale: Unit errors can cause major paediatric overdoses. Conversion and independent verification are essential.

questions.sectionLabel: Complex Medication, Chronic Illness and Discharge Care
questions.stem: A child with cystic fibrosis is preparing to return to school. Which discharge plan is most appropriate?

options.text: Coordinate medicines, airway-clearance needs, nutrition, school support, warning signs and follow-up responsibilities.
Provide the family with general advice only.
Advise the child to avoid all school activities.
Leave all planning to the parent.

questions.rationale: Children with complex conditions require coordinated plans across home, school and healthcare services.

questions.sectionLabel: Complex Medication, Chronic Illness and Discharge Care
questions.stem: A child with diabetes is admitted repeatedly because of missed insulin at school. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Assume the family is non-compliant.
Review the care plan with the family, school staff and diabetes team, and clarify responsibilities and access barriers.
Increase the insulin dose.
Tell the child to manage independently.

questions.rationale: Repeated admissions may indicate coordination or access problems rather than deliberate non-adherence.

questions.sectionLabel: Complex Medication, Chronic Illness and Discharge Care
questions.stem: Which information is most important in a paediatric emergency action plan?

options.text: The child's full developmental history.
Only the diagnosis.
Specific warning signs, immediate actions, medicine doses, emergency contacts and escalation steps.
A general statement to seek help if worried.

questions.rationale: A practical action plan must tell caregivers exactly what to recognise and do.

questions.sectionLabel: Complex Medication, Chronic Illness and Discharge Care
questions.stem: A parent can repeat medication instructions but cannot demonstrate use of an inhaler spacer. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Document that education is complete.
Ask the child to teach the parent later.
Provide another leaflet only.
Repeat and adapt teaching, then reassess using return demonstration.

questions.rationale: Practical equipment use should be confirmed by demonstration, not verbal recall alone.

questions.sectionLabel: Complex Medication, Chronic Illness and Discharge Care
questions.stem: A child with congenital heart disease tires during feeding and has poor weight gain. Which discharge support is most appropriate?

options.text: A coordinated plan for paced feeding, growth monitoring, medicines, warning signs and follow-up.
Advice to finish feeds quickly.
No school or community involvement.
Routine discharge without additional planning.

questions.rationale: Complex chronic care requires practical and coordinated support for feeding, growth and deterioration risk.

questions.sectionLabel: Complex Medication, Chronic Illness and Discharge Care
questions.stem: Why must infusion compatibility be checked in children receiving multiple IV medicines?

options.text: Compatibility matters only in adults.
Limited vascular access and small fluid volumes increase the risk of incompatible medicines mixing in the same line.
Smart pumps prevent incompatibility.
Incompatibility affects colour only.

questions.rationale: Paediatric patients often have restricted access, making compatibility checks especially important.

questions.sectionLabel: Complex Medication, Chronic Illness and Discharge Care
questions.stem: A nurse calculates a dose that exceeds the documented maximum safe dose. What should happen?

options.text: Administer because the weight-based calculation is correct.
Give half the dose.
Withhold the medicine and clarify the order before administration.
Ask the parent to approve the larger dose.

questions.rationale: A dose exceeding the maximum safe limit requires clarification, even if the weight-based calculation appears correct.

questions.sectionLabel: Complex Medication, Chronic Illness and Discharge Care
questions.stem: A child with complex disability has care from several services, but no one is clearly responsible for equipment review. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Assume the family will coordinate the services.
Order replacement equipment independently.
Wait until the equipment fails.
Raise the gap, clarify responsibilities and ensure a coordinated plan is documented.

questions.rationale: Clear accountability across services reduces fragmented care and preventable harm.

questions.sectionLabel: Complex Medication, Chronic Illness and Discharge Care
questions.stem: Which discharge method best confirms a family's understanding of seizure first aid?

options.text: Use teach-back and ask the caregivers to describe and demonstrate the emergency response.
Ask whether the explanation was clear.
Provide a poster.
Ask the child to sign the plan.

questions.rationale: Teach-back and demonstration reveal misunderstandings before discharge.

questions.sectionLabel: Complex Medication, Chronic Illness and Discharge Care
questions.stem: A child with asthma is discharged with several inhalers. What is the most important nursing check?

options.text: Whether the labels are attractive.
That the child and caregiver can identify each medicine, explain when it is used and demonstrate correct technique.
Whether the child prefers one device.
Whether the family has used inhalers before.

questions.rationale: Safe self-management requires correct medicine identification, timing and technique.

questions.sectionLabel: Complex Medication, Chronic Illness and Discharge Care
questions.stem: A school nurse has not received the updated rescue-medication plan for a child with epilepsy. What should the hospital nurse do?

options.text: Assume the parent will explain the change.
Tell the child to carry verbal instructions.
Ensure the current plan is communicated through approved channels before school attendance.
Delay discharge indefinitely.

questions.rationale: Continuity of care requires accurate communication across settings.

questions.sectionLabel: Complex Medication, Chronic Illness and Discharge Care
questions.stem: Which finding suggests that a family may need additional discharge support?

options.text: They ask appropriate questions.
They request written information.
They prefer a professional interpreter.
They cannot explain warning signs or demonstrate equipment use despite education.

questions.rationale: Inability to apply the plan indicates that discharge education is incomplete.

questions.sectionLabel: Complex Medication, Chronic Illness and Discharge Care
questions.stem: A child with chronic illness is approaching adolescence. What should care planning increasingly include?

options.text: Developmentally appropriate self-management and participation while maintaining family support.
Immediate transfer of all responsibility to the child.
Exclusion of parents from every discussion.
Focus only on medication adherence.

questions.rationale: Growing autonomy should be supported gradually according to maturity and ability.

questions.sectionLabel: Complex Medication, Chronic Illness and Discharge Care
questions.stem: A family uses a complementary product alongside prescribed medicines. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Ignore it because it is not prescribed.
Assess what is being used, check for interactions and communicate concerns to the appropriate team.
Tell the family to stop everything immediately.
Document only if an adverse effect occurs.

questions.rationale: A complete medication history includes non-prescription and complementary products.

questions.sectionLabel: Complex Medication, Chronic Illness and Discharge Care
questions.stem: Which outcome best reflects safe chronic-care coordination?

options.text: The family receives one hospital leaflet.
The primary clinician holds all information.
Responsibilities, medicines, equipment, emergency plans and follow-up are clear across home, school and health services.
The child manages all care independently.

questions.rationale: Coordination requires clear roles and communication across settings.

questions.sectionLabel: Complex Medication, Chronic Illness and Discharge Care
questions.stem: Which outcome best demonstrates safe paediatric medication and discharge practice?

options.text: The medicine chart is complete.
The family states that they are confident.
The discharge summary is printed.
Calculations are verified, technology is checked critically, and caregivers can safely perform the plan before discharge.

questions.rationale: Safe practice combines technical accuracy with demonstrated caregiver capability.

questions.sectionLabel: Safeguarding, Communication and Culturally Safe Care
questions.stem: An adolescent asks to speak privately about medication and home safety. During the discussion, the adolescent discloses immediate risk of harm. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Explain the limits of confidentiality, ensure immediate safety and follow the safeguarding pathway.
Promise complete confidentiality.
Tell the adolescent to speak with the parent first.
Delay action until the next appointment.

questions.rationale: Privacy should be respected, but immediate safety concerns require disclosure through approved safeguarding processes.

questions.sectionLabel: Safeguarding, Communication and Culturally Safe Care
questions.stem: A parent with limited English must consent to a complex procedure. Which approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Use an older sibling to interpret.
Arrange a professional interpreter, explain the procedure clearly and check understanding.
Ask the parent to sign the form first.
Rely on gestures and translated leaflets only.

questions.rationale: Professional interpretation is required for complex and high-risk communication.

questions.sectionLabel: Safeguarding, Communication and Culturally Safe Care
questions.stem: Which finding should raise a safeguarding concern?

options.text: A bruise over the shin of an active child.
A parent asking repeated questions.
Injuries inconsistent with the explanation, delayed presentation and fearful behaviour.
A child becoming upset during examination.

questions.rationale: Inconsistent injury history, delayed presentation and behavioural indicators may suggest abuse or neglect.

questions.sectionLabel: Safeguarding, Communication and Culturally Safe Care
questions.stem: A nurse suspects abuse but is uncertain whether the evidence is conclusive. What is the safest action?

options.text: Wait until proof is available.
Confront the caregiver immediately.
Discuss the case with other families.
Document objective findings and follow local legal and organisational reporting requirements.

questions.rationale: Nurses report concerns through approved pathways; they do not need to prove abuse independently.

questions.sectionLabel: Safeguarding, Communication and Culturally Safe Care
questions.stem: A child with a trauma history becomes distressed when staff approach with equipment. What is the best nursing response?

options.text: Use calm communication, explain each step, offer safe choices and minimise unnecessary restraint.
Proceed quickly without explanation.
Ask the parent to leave.
Tell the child that cooperation is required.

questions.rationale: Predictability, choice and calm communication are central to trauma-informed care.

questions.sectionLabel: Safeguarding, Communication and Culturally Safe Care
questions.stem: Which statement best describes assent?

options.text: A legal document signed by every child.
The child's developmentally appropriate agreement to participate in care, alongside legal consent where required.
A replacement for parental consent.
A process used only with adolescents.

questions.rationale: Children should be involved in decisions according to maturity, even when legal consent is provided by an adult.

questions.sectionLabel: Safeguarding, Communication and Culturally Safe Care
questions.stem: A family requests a cultural practice that does not create clinical risk. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Decline because hospital routines must be identical.
Document the family as non-compliant.
Explore and accommodate the practice where possible.
Avoid further discussion.

questions.rationale: Culturally safe care asks rather than assumes and accommodates safe preferences.

questions.sectionLabel: Safeguarding, Communication and Culturally Safe Care
questions.stem: A child with hearing impairment needs education about a new medicine. What is the best approach?

options.text: Speak more loudly.
Address the caregiver only.
Provide a standard leaflet.
Use accessible communication such as visual support or an interpreter, and confirm understanding.

questions.rationale: Communication should be adapted to the child's needs and understanding verified.

questions.sectionLabel: Safeguarding, Communication and Culturally Safe Care
questions.stem: An adolescent requests privacy, but the parent insists on remaining in the room. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Explain the value of private adolescent assessment and arrange it within legal and safety limits.
Always follow the parent's preference.
Refuse to see the adolescent.
Ask security to remove the parent.

questions.rationale: Adolescents should have appropriate opportunities for confidential discussion.

questions.sectionLabel: Safeguarding, Communication and Culturally Safe Care
questions.stem: Which documentation is most appropriate when safeguarding concerns arise?

options.text: A definitive diagnosis of abuse.
Objective descriptions of injuries, statements and observed behaviour, without speculation.
Emotional language about the caregiver.
No documentation until authorities confirm the concern.

questions.rationale: Safeguarding documentation should be factual, precise and timely.

questions.sectionLabel: Safeguarding, Communication and Culturally Safe Care
questions.stem: A caregiver becomes defensive when the nurse asks about an unexplained injury. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Argue until the caregiver admits responsibility.
End the assessment.
Remain calm, continue objective assessment and follow the safeguarding pathway.
Promise that no report will be made.

questions.rationale: The nurse should maintain safety, professionalism and objective documentation rather than investigate through confrontation.

questions.sectionLabel: Safeguarding, Communication and Culturally Safe Care
questions.stem: A child refuses a non-urgent procedure after receiving an age-appropriate explanation. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Use restraint immediately.
Ignore the refusal because legal consent was obtained.
Threaten a more painful alternative.
Explore the child's concern, involve the caregiver and team, and consider whether the procedure can be adapted or delayed safely.

questions.rationale: Assent and trauma-informed care require attention to the child's distress and participation where clinically possible.

questions.sectionLabel: Safeguarding, Communication and Culturally Safe Care
questions.stem: Which statement about confidentiality with adolescents is most accurate?

options.text: Privacy should be respected, but confidentiality has limits when there is serious risk or legal obligation.
Everything discussed must remain confidential.
Parents must receive every detail.
Confidentiality applies only after age 18.

questions.rationale: The nurse should explain confidentiality honestly, including its safety limits.

questions.sectionLabel: Safeguarding, Communication and Culturally Safe Care
questions.stem: A family relies on a child to interpret complex safeguarding information. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Continue because the child understands the family language.
Use a professional interpreter and protect the child from the interpreting role.
Ask the child to summarise only.
Avoid discussing safeguarding.

questions.rationale: Children should not be used to interpret complex or sensitive information.

questions.sectionLabel: Safeguarding, Communication and Culturally Safe Care
questions.stem: A child with developmental disability shows a sudden change in behaviour and fear around one caregiver. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Assume the behaviour is part of the disability.
Ask the caregiver to explain the behaviour and accept the answer.
